extracted.subtask_description: criteria for hard claim-matching cases the standard bank misses

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbatim claim-language echo as self-citation red flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Score how closely the reference's phrasing mirrors the claim's own idiosyncratic drafting (unusual word order, the exact grouping/order of a list, distinctive coined terms) rather than describing the same substance in independent, naturally-occurring technical prose. Score 0-4 where 4 = the passage reads as a genuinely independent third party's own description of the underlying technology (different vocabulary, different organization, but the same substance), and 0 = the passage is a near word-for-word parrot of the claim's specific phrasing and list ordering, which is a signature of the applicant's own related disclosure (parent/continuation spec, own prior filing) being surfaced by lexical similarity rather than a genuine independent anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In several hard cases the distractor was an almost word-for-word match to the claim's own phrasing (identical multi-item list order, identical clause structure) while the true match used unrelated, independently-worded prose for the same underlying concept; near-perfect verbatim overlap with the claim's specific drafting idiosyncrasies is itself suspicious rather than reassuring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush/laundry-list dilution versus focused dedicated disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claimed feature appears as one interchangeable entry inside a long, heterogeneous, boilerplate enumeration ("may further comprise X, Y, Z... or any commercially available standard selected from the group consisting of...") versus as the subject of a focused, dedicated sentence or worked example. Score 0-4: 4 = the reference is substantively about this specific feature (a definitional statement, a worked example, a named embodiment built around it); 0 = the matching term is buried as one option among many dozens in an undifferentiated catch-all list with no signal that it was the one actually used or emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several hard cases had a distractor listing the exact target term (a standard, a material, an ingredient) inside a sprawling Markush-style or "and other conventional additives" list, while the true match discussed the same concept in a shorter, focused, dedicated statement — length/list-membership of the mention, not raw term presence, tracked the correct answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural/mechanism correspondence despite vocabulary mismatch
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the reference discloses the same underlying physical structure or operating mechanism as the claim (same arrangement of parts, same principle by which the result is achieved), independent of whether it uses the claim's specific words. Score 0-4: 4 = the mechanism (how the parts are arranged and interact to produce the effect) genuinely matches even if named differently; 0 = only the outcome-vocabulary or field-vocabulary overlaps while the actual mechanism disclosed is different or absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In multiple hard cases the true match, using none of the claim's specific nouns, described a structural arrangement (a permeable lattice/grate that both supports an object and lets liquid pass, a barrier core flanked symmetrically by matched layers) that mechanically mirrors the claim, while the vocabulary-rich distractor named the right components but arranged them differently or for a different purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural phase or system-location context identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the disclosed action occurs at the same stage of a pipeline, in the same operating mode, or in the same physically-located component that the claim specifies (e.g., stationary casing vs. rotating blade; image-domain vs. projection-domain processing; idle-mode periodic monitoring vs. initial acquisition search; a gateway bridging two networks vs. an endpoint device). Score 0-4: 4 = the located component/stage/mode is the same one named or implied by the claim; 0 = the reference performs an analogous-sounding operation but at a different pipeline stage, in a different mode, or hosted in a different named component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard cases repeatedly showed a distractor with a near-identical trigger/threshold comparison or action verb but situated in the wrong place (blade cooling vs. casing cooling, conversion happening at the end-device vs. at the gateway, projection-domain subtraction vs. image-domain subtraction, cell-search termination vs. neighbor-cell-measurement skipping) — same-sounding condition, wrong locus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent claim-chain referential consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: For a dependent-claim limitation that refers back to a component or concept already named earlier in the claim chain ("the light signals", "the negative electrode collector", "the packets ... of speech data"), verify the candidate passage is tied to that SAME earlier-established entity/context, not a generic or free-standing instance of the phrase untethered to it. Score 0-4: 4 = the passage is explicitly anchored to the same antecedent role/context as established upstream in the claim; 0 = the passage matches the incremental new words in isolation but describes an unrelated or differently-contextualized instance (e.g. the collector is tied to the positive electrode, the light is a generic indicator not the communication channel established earlier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases where a distractor was an almost perfect lexical match for the added dependent clause alone (e.g. an exact Markush list of collector metals, or 'light source... to emit light signals') were nonetheless wrong because they weren't shown to attach to the specific antecedent entity/role (negative electrode specifically, the previously-established communication-light function) that the claim chain had already fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting/aggregation-architecture correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the computational/data-structure shape of what is being tracked: a single shared incrementing/decrementing (differential) value between two competing entities, or a single aggregate/summary value (a count, a syndrome), versus independent per-item values (one counter or flag per object). Score 0-4: 4 = the reference's counting/aggregation scheme has the same shape as the claim's (e.g. one shared competing counter, one aggregate summary signal); 0 = the reference reuses the same count/counter/reliability vocabulary but implements a structurally different scheme (independent per-object counts, a per-bit array of flags, rather than the claimed shared/aggregate value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several hard cases had a distractor using near-identical counting vocabulary ("counters that count accesses", "one reliability bit ... per bit") that in fact described independent per-object or per-bit tallies, while the true match — despite different terminology (an LRU access-order record, a logical-AND aggregate confidence signal) — matched the claim's specific shared/aggregate counting architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical or arithmetic relationship fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the reference actually demonstrates the specific mathematical/arithmetic relationship the claim requires (an equivalence, a complementary computation, a linearity property, an inverse count relationship) rather than merely mentioning the related quantities without connecting them that way. Score 0-4: 4 = the reference works through or states the actual relationship (e.g., shows that a difference/complement/division produces the claimed value or comparison); 0 = the reference states superficially related numbers or operations but never establishes the specific relationship the claim depends on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In hard cases, a distractor that literally restated the claimed range or listed disjoint values lost to a true match that derived the claimed quantity via an arithmetic complement (a stated contaminant percentage implying the purity percentage) or a stated equivalence/linearity property justifying why an operation in one domain equals the claimed operation in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-type and reagent/component functional-role classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that the reference's process belongs to the same specific technical category the claim recites (e.g., solution polymerization vs. aqueous emulsion/suspension polymerization) and that a named reagent plays the same functional role in its reaction system as the claimed component (e.g., a two-part activator/hardener vs. a UV photoinitiator), not merely that generic process/reagent vocabulary overlaps. Score 0-4: 4 = same process category and same reagent role; 0 = superficially similar procedural language (dropwise addition, initiator, percentage loadings) but for a differently-classified process or a reagent serving a different function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hard case's distractor described a detailed, numerically rich procedure that was nonetheless an aqueous emulsion-type process, not the claimed solution process; another distractor's in-range percentage figure belonged to a UV photoinitiator rather than the two-part activator system the claim and true match shared — procedural detail and numeric overlap did not imply the same process/role classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method step-sequence match versus static end-state description
rubrics_metrics.description: For method/process claims reciting an ordered sequence of steps, check whether the reference discloses an analogous ordered sequence of process actions (providing, then depositing, then etching, then depositing again) rather than only describing the resulting static structure. Score 0-4: 4 = the reference lays out an analogous multi-step fabrication sequence with comparable step-to-step dependency; 0 = the reference only shows a finished structural/geometric result (a shape or pattern that exists) without teaching the sequence of steps that produced it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One hard case's distractor was a single static sentence describing a concave pattern's existence, while the true match — using different materials/terms — laid out the same kind of ordered multi-step manufacturing sequence (form/deposit/etch/deposit) that a method claim actually requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanistic substantiation versus boilerplate outcome assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish passages that assert the claimed result as a generic, hedged, marketing-style benefit statement (typical of background/summary sections, often listing multiple unrelated benefits with words like "may", "can", "prophylactically") from passages that explain the underlying scientific/causal mechanism by which the specific embodiment would produce that result. Score 0-4: 4 = the reference explains the operative mechanism that would produce the claimed effect, even without using the claim's exact outcome word; 0 = the reference merely declares the exact outcome in generic promotional language without any mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hard case's distractor stated the claimed effect (e.g. reduces inflammation) almost verbatim in a broad, hedged, benefits-listing sentence, while the true match explained the actual physiological mechanism (modulating neural activity/function) that would produce that same effect without ever using the claim's outcome word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness and primacy of disclosed role versus hedged/incidental mention
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the reference identifies the matching element as the dedicated, intended component in a definite, unhedged way, versus a speculative, secondary, or dual-purpose characterization ("what may be", "could also serve as", a layer whose primary function is something else). Score 0-4: 4 = the element is named as the definite, purpose-built component; 0 = the correspondence rests on a hedged, speculative, or incidental repurposing of a component whose stated primary function is different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hard case's distractor named the right material for the right general function only inside a hedged aside ("a portion of the hard mask film forms what may be the capacitive dielectric") for a component whose primary role was something else, while the true match named the same material as the definite, dedicated dielectric layer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence versus transience of the claimed property or state
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim requires a property (e.g., accommodating relative movement, permitting flow) to exist in the assembly's completed/operative state, check whether the reference's disclosed property persists after assembly/fastening/curing is complete, or is only a transient feature of an intermediate installation stage that is eliminated once the assembly is finished. Score 0-4: 4 = the property is described as a permanent, operative feature of the finished assembly; 0 = the property is explicitly described as existing only before a completion event (before fastening/curing/locking) and disappearing afterward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hard case's distractor described components that could move relative to each other only before fasteners were tightened (i.e., the movement disappears in the final assembled state), while the true match's limiting-tab mechanism described a movement allowance that persists as an operative feature of the completed, fastened joint, matching the claim's requirement of ongoing accommodation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidirectional round-trip conduit identity
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim limitation requiring the same intermediary component to handle both an outbound action and its corresponding return/response (e.g., directing a request through X and receiving the reply through X), check whether the reference shows that single component handling both directions, versus a one-way relay chain or a request path with an unaddressed or different return path. Score 0-4: 4 = the same named intermediary is shown carrying traffic in both directions; 0 = the reference only shows a one-directional multi-hop relay (or the direction opposite to what's needed) with no indication the same component completes the round trip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hard case's distractor described a multi-hop relay chain (device to gateway to server to server) for outbound requests only, while the true match described a single control-unit-type intermediary relaying data inbound from devices AND signals back out to them through that same node, matching a claim requiring one conduit for both directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference's own cross-domain generality or extensibility statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the reference itself states that its disclosed mechanism is generically applicable across a class of analogous applications ("can be applied to any type of X, including...") even when its illustrated examples are drawn from a different specific field than the claim's, versus a reference whose matching-field vocabulary is not accompanied by any such generalizing statement and may be tied to a narrow, non-analogous specific use. Score 0-4: 4 = the reference explicitly broadens its own teaching to a general mechanism spanning analogous fields that would reasonably include the claimed field; 0 = the reference's matching vocabulary is confined to a narrow specific application with no generalizing language, even if that application happens to share the claim's field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hard case's true match, illustrated only with vehicle-hatch examples, explicitly stated its drive mechanism "can be applied to any type of access opening," while the field-matching distractor (doors/drawers/flaps) gave no indication its disclosed mechanism was the same generically-extensible one, despite naming the claim's exact furniture-part vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic template mimicry with substituted core technical variable
rubrics_metrics.description: When a distractor's sentence closely mirrors the claim's own grammatical template (subject-verb-object skeleton: "a controller ... determine a condition ... based on ... a profile") check whether the specific technical variable/parameter the claim names (e.g., frequency content of an electrical signal) is the one actually filling that slot in the reference, or whether a different, only superficially-analogous variable (e.g., a mechanical torque profile) has been substituted in. Score 0-4: 4 = the core named variable/parameter matches, regardless of how differently the surrounding sentence is phrased; 0 = the sentence structure closely parallels the claim but the substantive variable plugged into the key slot is a different physical quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hard case's distractor paraphrased the claim's exact sentence template almost clause-for-clause but swapped the claimed 'frequency content of an electrical parameter' for a 'combustion torque profile,' while the true match, phrased completely differently, actually demonstrated frequency-domain behavior of an electrical signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualized multi-part correspondence versus collective/aggregate description
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim names two or more distinct sub-elements with specific relational or positional roles (a first X and a second Y, an anterior part and a posterior part), check whether the reference maintains that same individualized, role-specific correspondence between distinct named parts, or instead describes the parts collectively/interchangeably without preserving which part plays which role. Score 0-4: 4 = the reference individually identifies each counterpart part and its specific role, matching the claim's differentiated naming; 0 = the reference describes the parts only as an undifferentiated group performing a shared function, collapsing the claim's role distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hard case's distractor described 'the leaflets' collectively closing against 'opposing side walls' without distinguishing which leaflet engages which side, while the true match specifically identified one leaflet against one named surface and the other leaflet against the other named surface, preserving the claim's first/second role distinction.
